CausalChain: Stress conditions (e.g., hypoxia, metabolic stress) -> Reduced tRNA methylation (NSUN2 suppression) and activated nucleases (e.g., ANG, ALKBH3 activity) -> Increased production of specific tRFs -> Translocation of these tRFs into mitochondria -> Direct interaction with mitochondrial ribosomes or mRNAs -> Modulation of mitochondrial protein synthesis for oxidative phosphorylation -> Adjusted energy metabolism enhancing cell survival under stress.
Hypothesis: Stress‐induced tRNA‐derived fragments translocate into mitochondria and directly regulate mitochondrial translation, thereby reprogramming oxidative phosphorylation to support cancer cell survival under hypoxic and metabolic stress conditions.
Abstract: Recent studies have illuminated the diverse roles of tRNA‐derived fragments (tRFs) in regulating mRNA stability, protein translation, and cellular stress responses in cancers and viral infections. We propose a novel mechanism whereby stress‐induced tRFs directly modulate mitochondrial translation. Under hypoxic or metabolic stress conditions, decreased tRNA methylation and elevated activities of specific nucleases result in the biogenesis of distinct tRF populations. We hypothesize that a subset of these tRFs translocate into mitochondria, where they interact with mitochondrial ribosomal subunits or mitochondrial mRNAs, fine‐tuning the synthesis of oxidative phosphorylation proteins. This modulation of mitochondrial translation would reprogram energy metabolism, enhancing cell survival under adverse conditions and contributing to tumor progression. The present hypothesis provides new avenues for exploring tRFs as regulators of mitochondrial function with potential implications in cancer metabolism and therapy.
